overview: The Tang dynasty is considered China's golden age, marked by cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist flourishing, poetic achievement and international trade. Chang'an became one of the world's largest cities, connected by the Silk Road to Central Asia, India and Persia.

items.text: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, produced using woodblock printing.
The first written warning of gunpowder's power appears in a Daoist alchemical text, describing a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burst into flame.
The great poets Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei create masterpieces of Chinese verse.
Buddhist cave temples at Dunhuang filled with murals and sculptures.
True porcelain, the white Xing wares of Hebei, is made, though it remained rare and precious.
The monk Xuanzang travels to India, returning in 645 with Buddhist texts that he translates.
Christianity arrives in Chang'an with the missionary Alopen; the Xi'an Stele of 781 records its reception.
Chang'an reaches a population of about one million, with foreign merchants, monks and diplomats.
Tea drinking becomes widespread; Lu Yu writes the Classic of Tea.
Silk Road trade connects China to Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.
Tang poetry became the standard for later Chinese literature.
Overseas Chinese still call a Chinatown a Tangrenjie, the street of the Tang people.

fall.text: The An Lushan Rebellion of 755 fatally weakened the dynasty; regional military governors gained power, and the last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen in 907.
